description: The synagogue, the Amidah, Tenakh as Written Law and Talmud as Oral Law.
content_html:
The Synagogue: Centre of Jewish Life

The synagogue is the heart of Jewish communal life. The Hebrew word means “house of assembly,” and synagogues serve as places for worship, Torah study, education and social support. Although the Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed in 70 CE, the prophet Ezekiel had already described G‑d as a “little sanctuary” for the people in exile (Ezekiel 11:16), giving religious authority to local places of prayer far from the Temple.

On entering a synagogue, worshippers face the eastern wall, oriented towards Jerusalem, the direction of prayer. The building’s design communicates core Jewish beliefs through its artefacts and layout.

Key Fact

Every synagogue contains four essential interior features: the Ark (Aron Kodesh) housing the Torah scrolls; the Bimah (raised reading platform); the Ner Tamid (Eternal Light); and the Sefer Torah (handwritten Torah scroll). A Mikveh (ritual immersion pool) is an important communal facility but is a separate building, not part of the synagogue interior itself.

Features and Their Significance

The Ark stands at the front of the synagogue and is treated with great reverence. Congregants rise when it is opened, reflecting the belief that the Torah is the Word of G‑d. Above or near the Ark burns the Ner Tamid, a lamp that never goes out. This recalls the menorah that burned perpetually in the ancient Temple and symbolises G‑d’s eternal presence with the Jewish people.

The Bimah stands in the centre or at the front. The Torah is carried from the Ark to the Bimah in a procession, and congregants may touch the Sefer Torah with their prayer book or tallit as it passes — a sign of reverence. The Torah is then unrolled and chanted aloud using a pointer called a yad, so the sacred text is never touched directly by bare fingers.

Synagogues have no images or statues of G‑d or humans because Jewish law (based on Exodus 20:4) forbids representations of G‑d. This distinguishes synagogue interiors from churches and reflects the belief that G‑d is beyond all human representation. Stained glass may include geometric patterns or Hebrew lettering, but never human or divine figures.

In an Orthodox synagogue, men and women sit separately — women in a gallery or behind a partition called the mechitzah. Services are conducted entirely in Hebrew, and only men may lead prayers. The Bimah is traditionally in the centre of the room.

In Reform synagogues, men and women sit together. English may be used alongside Hebrew, and women can lead services and become rabbis. The Bimah is usually at the front, more similar to a church layout. Both communities share the core artefacts — the Ark, Ner Tamid and Sefer Torah — but interpret how services are conducted very differently.

Prayer in Judaism

Prayer is central to Jewish worship. The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our G‑d, the Lord is one,” is the defining affirmation of Jewish faith and is recited morning and evening. Deuteronomy 10:12–13 commands Jews to serve G‑d “with all your heart and with all your soul.”

Jews traditionally pray three times a day: Shacharit (morning), Mincha (afternoon) and Ma’ariv (evening). These times echo the sacrifices offered in the ancient Temple. A minyan — a quorum of ten adult Jews — is traditionally required for communal prayer. In Orthodox communities, only men count towards a minyan; many Reform congregations count women too.

Key Fact

The Amidah (“the standing prayer”) is recited three times daily. It consists of nineteen blessings (in weekday form): praise of G‑d, petitions for needs such as health, sustenance and justice, and thanksgiving. Jews stand and face Jerusalem while saying it, and Orthodox Jews sway slightly (shuckling) as an expression of devotion.

Private prayer is also important. Jews may say tehillim (Psalms) spontaneously, recite the Shema before sleep, say Grace after meals (Birkat Hamazon), and offer personal prayers in their own words. Men in Orthodox communities wear a kippah (head covering) and use a tallit (prayer shawl) to show reverence before G‑d. Tefillin (small boxes containing Torah verses) are bound to the arm and forehead during morning prayer, following Deuteronomy 6:8.

Judaism is a domestic religion as much as a synagogue one. A mezuzah — a small scroll containing the Shema — is fixed to the doorpost of Jewish homes (based on Deuteronomy 6:9), reminding the household of G‑d’s presence. Shabbat candles are lit by the woman of the house on Friday evening, and blessings are recited over wine and bread (challah). Teaching children to pray at home is itself a religious duty, rooted in Deuteronomy 6:7: “Teach them diligently to your children.”

The Tenakh: Written Law

The Tenakh is the complete Hebrew Bible. Its name is an acronym from three sections: Torah (the five books of Moses), Neviim (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings). In Judaism, the Torah holds the highest authority — it contains the laws given by G‑d to Moses at Sinai and forms the foundation of Jewish faith and practice.

The Sefer Torah is a handwritten copy of the Torah produced by a trained scribe. It is treated as the most sacred object in the synagogue: dressed in a velvet cover, adorned with silver ornaments, and carried in procession. The Chumash is the same text in printed book form, used for personal study.

The Talmud: Oral Law

The Talmud is the record of the Oral Law. Jewish tradition holds that G‑d gave Moses both the Written Torah and the oral explanations at Sinai. For centuries these interpretations were transmitted by memory; they were eventually compiled as the Mishnah (around 200 CE) and then the Gemara (discussions of the Mishnah), together forming the Talmud. The Talmud covers legal rulings, ethical guidance, and theological debate.

In synagogue worship, the Tenakh provides the scriptural readings that structure every service. The weekly Torah portion (parashah) is read on Shabbat mornings, Mondays and Thursdays. The Haftarah (a reading from Neviim) follows. The Talmud is studied continuously — many Jews follow the Daf Yomi cycle, studying one page per day. Together, the Written and Oral Law guide every aspect of Jewish life.
exam_tip_html: When answering ‘Describe’ or ‘Outline’ questions about the synagogue, make sure you name specific interior features (Ark, Bimah, Ner Tamid, Sefer Torah) rather than describing them vaguely — note that the Mikveh is a separate communal facility, not part of the synagogue interior. The 6-mark ‘Explain’ question often targets differences between Orthodox and Reform practice — always specify which denomination is doing what. A common mistake is confusing the Tenakh with the Talmud: remember that the Tenakh is the Written Law (Torah, Neviim, Ketuvim) and the Talmud is the Oral Law (Mishnah + Gemara). The 15-mark Discuss question may ask whether communal or private worship matters most — use both synagogue sources (Amidah, minyan) and home-based examples (Shema, mezuzah) for a balanced answer. Correct spelling of technical terms such as “Amidah,” “Ner Tamid” and “Talmud” is rewarded on the extended response.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The synagogue is the centre of Jewish communal life, containing the Ark, Bimah, Ner Tamid and Sefer Torah; Orthodox and Reform communities share these features but differ significantly in how services are conducted, including the separation of men and women.
  • Prayer takes place three times daily; the Amidah (nineteen blessings recited standing towards Jerusalem) and the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) are the two most important prayers, used in both communal and private worship.
  • The Tenakh (Written Law: Torah, Neviim, Ketuvim) and the Talmud (Oral Law: Mishnah and Gemara) together provide the authoritative guidance for all Jewish belief and practice, used in both synagogue readings and daily study.

practice_questions.text: State what the Ner Tamid represents in a synagogue.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: G-d's eternal/constant presence; the menorah that burned in the Temple; the eternal nature of G-d. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the Bimah in a synagogue.
practice_questions.marks: The Bimah is a raised platform in the synagogue [1] from which the Torah is read aloud to the congregation during services [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three features found in a synagogue and their significance.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of: the Ark (Aron Kodesh) stores the Torah scrolls and is the focal point of worship; the Ner Tamid is a lamp that burns continuously, symbolising G-d's eternal presence; the Bimah is the raised reading platform where the Torah is chanted; the Sefer Torah is the handwritten Torah scroll, the holiest object in the synagogue; the lack of images reflects the commandment against representing G-d (Exodus 20:4). [3 marks — 1 mark each]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two differences between Orthodox and Reform synagogue worship.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In Orthodox synagogues men and women are separated by a mechitzah (partition), whereas in Reform synagogues they sit together. This reflects differing understandings of the binding nature of traditional law: Orthodox Jews follow halakha strictly, while Reform Jews believe the tradition can develop.
• Orthodox services are conducted entirely in Hebrew, with only men leading prayer. Reform services may use English alongside Hebrew, and women may lead prayers and become rabbis. Deuteronomy 10:12-13 calls all Jews to serve G-d wholeheartedly, but interpretations of how to do so differ.
• In Orthodox communities a minyan requires ten adult men; many Reform congregations count women towards the ten.
[6 marks — 3 marks per difference: 1 for a simple statement, 2 for development, 3 for a relevant source of wisdom]

practice_questions.text: 'The Talmud is more important to Jewish practice than the Tenakh.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Talmud provides the practical guidance on how to apply the Torah in daily life — without its rulings, Jews would not know how to observe Shabbat, keep kosher, or conduct lifecycle ceremonies. The Written Torah often gives only general principles.
• The Talmud has been the living law of diaspora Judaism for almost 2,000 years; Maimonides' legal codes and later authorities all build on Talmudic interpretation.
• For many Orthodox Jews, Talmud study is the highest religious act — the principle that Torah study equals all other commandments shows its practical primacy.

Arguments against:
• The Tenakh is the Written Law given by G-d to Moses at Sinai; the Talmud is a human (rabbinic) interpretation of that law. The Torah itself must logically take precedence.
• The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) and the core commandments all derive from the Tenakh, which is recited and read aloud at every synagogue service. The Sefer Torah is the most sacred object in the building.
• Without the Tenakh there would be nothing for the Talmud to interpret: the Written Law is the root, the Oral Law its branches.
• Some liberal Jewish movements give less authority to Talmudic rulings while still honouring the Tenakh.

Mastering: Both sides are fully developed with named sources (Deuteronomy 6:4, Talmud, Sefer Torah, rabbinic tradition), differences between Orthodox and Reform positions explored, and a justified conclusion that weighs which is more foundational to practice.
Secure: Clear arguments on both sides with relevant named sources and a conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points on both sides but sources limited or underdeveloped; conclusion present but not fully reasoned.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little or no reference to sources. [15 marks — SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Jews believe about the purpose of prayer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of: prayer enables communication with G-d; the three daily prayer times (Shacharit, Mincha, Ma'ariv) structure the whole day around G-d; prayer includes praise, confession, thanksgiving and supplication; the Amidah's nineteen blessings address G-d's greatness and human needs; private prayer (e.g. Psalms, Grace after meals) maintains a personal relationship with G-d. [3 marks — 1 mark each]

The Oral Law: rabbinic discussions of Torah, comprising the Mishnah and Gemara.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Ner Tamid mean and what does it symbolise?
flashcard_questions.a: Eternal Light; symbolises G-d's constant, unending presence.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Bimah used for?
flashcard_questions.a: A raised platform from which the Torah is read aloud in the synagogue.
The standing prayer of nineteen blessings, recited three times daily facing Jerusalem.

flashcard_questions.q: What prayer must Jews recite morning and evening, based on Deuteronomy 6:4?
flashcard_questions.a: The Shema — affirming that G-d is One.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are there no images of G-d in a synagogue?
flashcard_questions.a: Exodus 20:4 forbids making representations of G-d.

flashcard_questions.q: How does an Orthodox synagogue differ from a Reform synagogue in seating?
flashcard_questions.a: Orthodox: men and women separated by a mechitzah. Reform: mixed seating.

glossary_terms.definition: The Jewish place of assembly for worship, study and community life, sometimes called a shul.
The holy cabinet at the front of the synagogue which houses the Torah scrolls; the focal point of worship.
The 'Eternal Light', a lamp that burns continuously above the Ark in a synagogue, symbolising G-d's constant presence.
The raised platform in the synagogue from which the Torah is read aloud to the congregation.
A branch of Judaism that follows traditional law strictly, maintaining the Torah as binding in its entirety.
The Hebrew Bible, consisting of three sections: Torah (Law), Neviim (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings); also called the Written Law.
A handwritten Torah scroll used in synagogue readings, produced by a trained scribe (sofer) on parchment.
A printed version of the Torah for home or study use, often bound together with the targum or commentaries.
The authoritative collection of rabbinic discussion and interpretation of Jewish law; it comprises the Mishnah and Gemara and represents the Oral Law.
The tradition of interpretation and application of the Torah passed down from Sinai alongside the Written Torah, later compiled as the Mishnah and then the Talmud.
